headline: Nigerian Conservationist Wins Rolex Award for Saving Endangered Red Monkeys
meta_description: Rachel Ikemeh receives 2026 Rolex Award for protecting Niger Delta red colobus monkeys through community conservation efforts that doubled local populations.
summary_short: A Nigerian conservationist has won the prestigious 2026 Rolex Award for her work protecting the critically endangered Niger Delta red colobus monkey through innovative c…
body:
Nigerian conservationist Rachel Ikemeh has been named the 2026 Rolex Award laureate for her groundbreaking work protecting the critically endangered Niger Delta red colobus monkey, known locally as epieni. Working directly with communities across the Niger Delta region, Ikemeh has helped establish community-protected areas that are reversing decades of population decline. In a community-protected forest in Apoi, the epieni population doubled from 180–200 individuals in 2021 to around 400 by 2024—a remarkable turnaround for a primate listed among the world's 25 most endangered species. Ikemeh's 100,000 Swiss franc award will expand this success, funding four new community conservation areas and the region's first locally managed marine conservation area.

What makes Ikemeh's approach distinctive is how she has shifted local attitudes toward conservation. Communities that once feared the work would lead the government to seize their forest now view the epieni as a source of pride and identity. Several villages have even begun hosting other communities to learn from their conservation model—a grassroots replication that speaks to the program's success. "That change in attitude is the real conservation infrastructure," Ikemeh explained, emphasizing that community buy-in is as vital as any protected boundary.

Yet significant challenges remain. Outside the protected areas, threats persist from oil pollution, logging, hunting, and black sand mining. The epieni population, though growing, remains confined to a tiny range and vulnerable to disease outbreaks or regional unrest. Underlying economic pressures—poverty and lack of jobs—continue to drive unsustainable practices. Ikemeh's award recognizes not just past achievements but the potential of her community-centered model to sustain conservation long-term, offering a pathway where both people and endangered wildlife can thrive together.
quick_facts: Rachel Ikemeh wins 2026 Rolex Award for Niger Delta primate conservation
Epieni population doubled in Apoi protected forest between 2021 and 2024
Red colobus monkey listed among world's 25 most endangered primates
Award funding will establish four new community conservation areas
Communities now view endangered monkeys as source of village pride
